commenti.body:
It's interesting to me that you found the movie cynical; it wasn't really to my taste aesthetically but I thought it was very earnest. 

The whole movie has an open sincerity in it depiction of Owen's alienation and fear of acknowledging his/her true identity as Isabel. It never judges him for his lack of courage and it is always rooting for him to take the finally take leap. While it doesn't conclude definitively it does end with a moment of self discovery and revelation for Owen/Isabel which is a huge moment of forward progress for the character.

I agree that the writing in the move could have been tightened up. The mixing of the time lines, the device of him narrating by the fire, the plotting. . . there was room for improvement. Overall I really needed a bit more dynamism from at least one of the the characters. As it was it felt like an hour's worth of story stretched to 100 minutes. I'm also not really a fan of this post Everything Everywhere All at Once maximalist style and storytelling that has over taken a chunk of the indie space. In particular all of the early 00's nostalgia porn seemed to serve no purpose and turned me off. 

It also interesting to me that you didn't mention the clear allegory that's front and center in the movie. Like the second thing we see in the movie is kid Owen in the middle of a trans flag colored parachute and it doesn't get less subtle from there. The queer reading of the film which is very much the one intended by the filmmaker cuts against some of your takeaways about it being nothing but darkness.

Separately, I just disagree about the Maddie character. I found Lundy-Paine very charismatic and I was impressed by the way she evolved the character in the ten years later segment.

I agree the subtext of this film is clearly about queer identity. I dont see how that "cuts against" any of my points. Owen has a moment of self discovery but then goes right back to his old life because it was already too late for him. His final words are ones of meek apology for his outburst.

I disagree that it's cynical but you're totally right about everything else. I'd also add poor casting. The entire time they're supposed to be in high school was "Dear Evan Hansen" level ridiculous. And, the child actor who played young Owen doesn't look like Justice Smith even a little bit; they don't even have the same skin color.

> again, why did this film need to have 4th wall breaking?

Like or dislike it, a major aspect of I Saw the TV Glow is the broken fourth wall between the Pink Opaque and the two main characters. The protagonist literally attempts to insert themselves into a TV.

Having the characters directly address the audience watching the movie invites us into the immersive aspect of wondering which side of the 4th wall _we_ are currently occupying. It's asking us to unironically engage with the premise and imagine "What if we are wrong about our lives?"

From an allegorical perspective, the in-universe fourth wall break represents stepping away from the boring, mundane life that Maddie and Owen have been "assigned". Maddie accepts the call. Owen does not.

I Saw the TV Glow wants us to ask the same question of ourselves. For those of us who _do_ vibe with the messaging in I Saw the TV Glow, are _we_ willing to accept the call or not? Are we willing to engage directly with the movie on its own terms? Are we willing to risk letting go of our assigned life?

Or are we going to look at this as yet another childish piece of media that won't age well? And if so, will that be because _it_ doesn't age well or because _we_ won't age well?

Whether this is something you find interesting or boring is up to you. But the fourth wall breaks are fairly important to what it trying to accomplish. They aren't just tacked on for the sake of style.

This is one of the few movies I’ve seen that felt like a waste of time. Like I really wanted my time and money back by the end… however, I’m not saying it’s horrible. I think it had potential that it just completely wasted by under-developing the characters and mythology and generally just not taking the story far enough. I think I get what they were doing with the ending, but I still feel like they could’ve taken the story farther and not ended it so abruptly. If they extended the ending and just let us spend more time with both characters and developed them more it could’ve turned into something special.

My knee-jerk reaction is to be dismissive of your criticisms and call it shallow and generic without an attempt to truly engage with the material at hand. 

But I don't wanna be that guy.

And, despite how deeply this film hit my heart, it's the definition of a "divisive" film. It's not about plot. It's not about "answers." It's a meditative, heavily stylized exploration of repression that wants us to sit in the emotions it evokes. 

I can totally see people just NOT being on this films wavelength. 

But this film hit me like a truck and stirred up emotions and sensations in me regarding adolescence that honestly unzipped me. Old wounds, old feelings, old experiences, etc came rushing to the surface. 

While the film is obviously a queer narrative - the feelings it taps into are universal and powerful. The way Schoenbrun can tap directly into those complicated and nebulous and swirling maelstrom of teenage turmoil largely through visuals is stunning. It's never trite. It's never sensationalized or overly "movie" if you catch my meaning.

The first meeting of Owen and Maddy had me welling up because it felt so true, so honest - the crushing awkwardness of them both - how internal they both are - the repression they exude, the bid for connection they each make...I'm getting teary just typing this out, lol. 

  
I honestly can't see how anyone can call the film "cynical." I can see people thinking it's too sad or depressing, but "cynical?" It's one of the most honest, earnest, deeply felt and heart-on-the-sleeve bits of filmmaking I've seen in a while.

You know, you write pretty well and I can understand of this movie made you feel things but there’s just some things you can’t overlook. The acting and directing decisions in this movie were so Disney channel original movie or Netflix teen movie. It was completely insufferable to me. I think every aesthetic decision made by the director was diminutive toward the film in every way. 

Interesting ideas. Definitely original. Just very poorly done
